sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A network administrator creates a new network security group (NSG) named nsg-prod in the East US region. No custom security rules have been added to it yet. Which priority is assigned to the default rule that blocks all inbound traffic that is not allowed by another rule?
spiegazione: Correct: 65500 is the priority of the DenyAllInBound default rule, which denies traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to 0.0.0.0/0 on any protocol. Azure assigns default rules the highest priority numbers (lowest priority) so that custom rules are always processed first. Wrong: 4096 is the highest priority NUMBER you may assign to a custom rule, not a default rule. 65000 is the priority of AllowVNetInBound, which allows traffic between resources tagged VirtualNetwork. 65001 is the priority of AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound, which allows health probe traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: While scripting network security group rules with Az PowerShell, an engineer must supply a Priority value for every custom security rule that is added to an NSG. Which range of values does Azure accept for the priority of a user-defined security rule?
spiegazione: Correct: A security rule priority is a number between 100 and 4096. Rules are processed in priority order, and lower numbers are processed before higher numbers because lower numbers mean higher priority. Wrong: 1 through 1000 understates the floor and the ceiling; priorities below 100 are rejected. 100 through 65000 is wrong because 65000 is reserved for the AllowVNetInBound/AllowVnetOutBound default rules; the custom range stops at 4096. 0 through 65500 is wrong for the same reason and because 0 is not a valid priority; 65500 is reserved for the DenyAllInBound/DenyAllOutBound default rules.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: In VNet1, the subnet named Subnet1 has the network security group NSG1 associated to it. VM1 resides in Subnet1, and VM1's network interface NIC1 has the network security group NSG2 associated to it. A client on the internet initiates a connection to VM1 over TCP port 443. In which order does Azure evaluate the two network security groups for this inbound flow?
opzione_a: NSG2 only, because a rule on a network interface always overrides the rules of the subnet
opzione_d: NSG1 and NSG2 are merged into a single rule set and evaluated together in priority order
spiegazione: Correct: For inbound traffic, Azure first processes the rules in the NSG associated with the subnet, and then processes the rules in the NSG associated with the network interface. Both NSGs must allow TCP 443 for the traffic to reach VM1; if NSG1 blocks the traffic, NSG2 never evaluates it. Wrong: A NIC-level NSG does not override a subnet-level NSG; both are enforced independently. NSG2 first, then NSG1 describes the OUTBOUND order, which is the reverse of inbound. The two NSGs are never merged into one rule set; each is evaluated separately, and priority numbers are only compared within a single NSG.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: VM2 has a network interface associated with a network security group named nsg-nic, and the subnet that hosts VM2 is associated with a network security group named nsg-subnet. nsg-nic contains an outbound rule at priority 200 that denies TCP port 80 to the Internet service tag. nsg-subnet contains no custom outbound rules. VM2 attempts to open an outbound HTTP connection to a public website. Which statement describes the outcome?
opzione_a: The traffic is denied by nsg-nic, and nsg-subnet never receives the traffic to evaluate it
opzione_b: The traffic is evaluated by nsg-subnet first, and because AllowInternetOutBound permits it, the connection succeeds
opzione_c: Both nsg-nic and nsg-subnet must contain a deny rule for the outbound traffic to be blocked
opzione_d: Outbound rules in a network interface NSG are ignored; only the subnet NSG filters outbound traffic
spiegazione: Correct: For outbound traffic, Azure evaluates the NSG associated with the network interface first, and then the NSG associated with the subnet. Because nsg-nic denies TCP 80 at priority 200, the traffic is dropped there and nsg-subnet never receives it. To deny outbound traffic, either one or both NSGs need a deny rule. Wrong: Evaluating nsg-subnet first is the inbound order, not the outbound order. Requiring both NSGs to deny is the inverse of how deny works: a single deny anywhere in the path is sufficient (it is ALLOW that must exist in both NSGs). NIC-level outbound rules are absolutely enforced; they are in fact evaluated before subnet-level outbound rules.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: An application security group named AsgLogic contains network interfaces that reside in VNet1. A second application security group named AsgDb contains network interfaces that reside in VNet2. An administrator attempts to create a security rule that specifies AsgLogic as the source and AsgDb as the destination. What is the result?
opzione_a: The configuration is not supported, because the network interfaces in both the source and destination application security groups must exist in the same virtual network
opzione_b: The rule is created successfully, but it applies only to the network interfaces that are in VNet1
opzione_c: The rule is created successfully, and Azure automatically creates a virtual network peering between VNet1 and VNet2
opzione_d: The rule is created successfully, provided that AsgLogic and AsgDb reside in the same resource group
spiegazione: Correct: A documented ASG constraint states that if you specify an application security group as the source and destination in a security rule, the network interfaces in both application security groups must exist in the same virtual network. Because AsgLogic spans VNet1 and AsgDb spans VNet2, the rule cannot be assigned. Wrong: The rule does not partially apply to VNet1 only; the configuration is rejected outright. Azure never creates virtual network peering implicitly as a side effect of a security rule. Resource group membership is irrelevant to this constraint; the boundary that matters is the virtual network, not the resource group.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A network security group named nsg-mgmt is associated with a subnet and contains the following inbound custom rules, in addition to the default rules: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source 203.0.113.10, destination Any, destination port 3389; priority 200, Deny, TCP, source Internet, destination Any, destination port 3389; priority 300, Allow, TCP, source Internet, destination Any, destination port 3389. A support technician at the public IP address 203.0.113.10 initiates an RDP connection to a VM in the subnet. Which rule determines the outcome?
opzione_a: The rule at priority 100 allows the connection
opzione_b: The rule at priority 200 denies the connection, because deny rules are always evaluated before allow rules
opzione_c: The rule at priority 300 allows the connection, because it is the last matching rule to be processed
opzione_d: The DenyAllInBound default rule at priority 65500 denies the connection
spiegazione: Correct: Rules are processed in priority order, lowest number first, and once traffic matches a rule, processing stops. The five-tuple of this flow (source 203.0.113.10, TCP, destination port 3389) matches the rule at priority 100, so the connection is allowed and no lower-priority rule is evaluated. Wrong: Azure does not give deny rules any inherent precedence; only the priority number determines order, so the rule at 200 is never reached. The rule at 300 is not evaluated either, and processing stops at the FIRST match, not the last. DenyAllInBound is only reached when no higher-priority rule matches, which is not the case here.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: A support engineer must view the aggregated set of rules from both the subnet NSG and the network interface NSG that apply to the network interface of a virtual machine named vm-1, by using the Effective security rules page in the Azure portal. Which condition must be satisfied for Azure to return the effective security rules?
opzione_a: The virtual machine must be in the running state
opzione_b: The virtual machine must be stopped (deallocated) so that the platform can recalculate the rule set
opzione_c: Virtual network flow logs must be enabled on the virtual network
opzione_d: A network security group must be associated with both the subnet and the network interface
spiegazione: Correct: Azure shows effective security rules for a network interface only when an NSG is associated with the network interface or its subnet, and the VM must be in the running state. Wrong: A deallocated VM is precisely the case where no effective rules are returned; the VM must be running, not stopped. Virtual network flow logs record traffic data for analysis but are not a prerequisite for viewing effective security rules. An NSG associated with BOTH the subnet and the NIC is not required: effective rules are returned when an NSG is associated with the network interface, the subnet, or both.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: The network security group associated with a virtual machine's network interface contains an outbound rule that allows TCP port 443 to the Internet service tag. No custom inbound rules have been created in that NSG. The virtual machine initiates an HTTPS request to a public website. What must be configured so that the response traffic from the website reaches the virtual machine?
opzione_a: An inbound rule that allows TCP port 443 from the Internet service tag
opzione_b: An inbound rule that allows the ephemeral port range 1024-65535 from the Internet service tag
opzione_c: No additional rule is required, because a flow record makes the network security group stateful
opzione_d: An inbound rule that allows traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag
spiegazione: Correct: A flow record is created for existing connections, and communication is allowed or denied based on the connection state of the flow record. This flow record is what makes an NSG stateful: if you allow outbound traffic on a port, you do not need a matching inbound rule for the response. An inbound rule is only needed when the communication is initiated externally. Wrong: An inbound rule allowing TCP 443 from Internet is unnecessary and would additionally expose the VM to externally initiated connections on that port. An inbound rule for the ephemeral port range is the classic stateless-firewall misconception; it is not needed and would be dangerously broad. AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound-style rules cover Azure health probe traffic, which is unrelated to the response of an outbound HTTPS session.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: Which statements accurately describe the default security rules that Azure creates in every network security group? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: AllowVNetInBound has priority 65000 and allows inbound traffic between resources that are covered by the VirtualNetwork service tag
opzione_b: Default security rules can be deleted from a network security group when they are not needed
opzione_c: AllowInternetOutBound has priority 65001 and allows outbound traffic to the Internet service tag
opzione_d: DenyAllInBound has priority 65500 and denies all inbound traffic that is not allowed by a higher-priority rule
opzione_e: Default security rules are processed before custom security rules within the same network security group
spiegazione: Correct: AllowVNetInBound (priority 65000) allows traffic from the VirtualNetwork tag to the VirtualNetwork tag on any protocol and port. AllowInternetOutBound (priority 65001) allows outbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet service tag. DenyAllInBound (priority 65500) denies traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to 0.0.0.0/0, so anything not explicitly allowed by a lower-numbered rule is dropped. Wrong: Default rules cannot be removed; you can only override them by creating custom rules with a higher priority (a lower number). Default rules are NOT processed first: Azure deliberately assigns them the lowest priority (the highest numbers, 65000-65500) so that custom rules in the 100-4096 range are always processed before them.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A cloud engineer is designing network segmentation for a multi-tier workload and plans to use application security groups (ASGs). Which statements about application security groups are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A network interface can be a member of multiple application security groups, up to the Azure limits
opzione_b: An application security group can be specified as the source or the destination of a network security group rule
opzione_c: All network interfaces assigned to an application security group must exist in the same virtual network as the first network interface that was assigned to that group
opzione_d: An application security group can be associated directly with a subnet, replacing the need for a network security group
opzione_e: An application security group must be associated with a network security group before it can be referenced in a security rule
spiegazione: Correct: A network interface can belong to more than one application security group, up to the documented Azure limits. An ASG is a valid value for the Source and the Destination of a security rule, which lets you write rules against workload roles instead of IP addresses. All NICs assigned to an ASG must exist in the same virtual network as the first NIC assigned to it; you cannot add NICs from different virtual networks to the same ASG. Wrong: An ASG cannot be associated with a subnet. An ASG only groups network interfaces; the filtering is still performed by a network security group associated with a subnet or a NIC. There is no association between an ASG and an NSG: you simply select the existing ASG in the Source or Destination of a rule, and the rule then applies to the network interfaces that are members of that group.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: Connectivity to a virtual machine is failing intermittently, and an administrator plans to use the IP flow verify capability of Azure Network Watcher to determine whether a packet is allowed or denied. Which statements about IP flow verify are correct? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: IP flow verify evaluates the rules of all network security groups applied to the virtual machine's network interface, whether the NSG is associated with the subnet or with the network interface
opzione_b: IP flow verify returns Access allowed or Access denied together with the name of the security rule responsible for the result
opzione_c: IP flow verify can be used to test rules that apply to ICMP traffic
opzione_d: A Network Watcher instance must exist in the Azure subscription and region of the virtual machine
opzione_e: IP flow verify evaluates the effective routes of the network interface to confirm the next hop for the packet
spiegazione: Correct: IP flow verify looks at the rules of all NSGs applied to a VM's network interface, regardless of whether the NSG is associated to the subnet or the NIC, and it also considers Azure Virtual Network Manager admin rules. It returns Access denied or Access allowed plus the name of the security rule that denied or allowed the traffic and a link to the NSG (no link is provided when a default rule is responsible). A Network Watcher instance is required in the subscription and region of the VM. Wrong: IP flow verify only tests TCP and UDP rules; to test ICMP traffic rules you must use NSG diagnostics instead. IP flow verify does not evaluate routing: it tests security and admin rules only. To confirm the next hop for a packet you would use the Next hop capability of Network Watcher.
tags: ip flow verify,network watcher,nsg,troubleshooting,effective security rules

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: You create a new network security group named nsg-app. You have not added any custom security rules to it. You review the default security rules that Azure created in the network security group. Select the correct value for each item.
spiegazione: Correct: AllowVNetInBound has priority 65000 and allows traffic from the VirtualNetwork tag to the VirtualNetwork tag. AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound has priority 65001 and allows traffic from the AzureLoadBalancer tag to 0.0.0.0/0, which is how Azure load balancer health probes reach the VM. DenyAllOutBound has priority 65500 and its action is Deny; it is the last outbound default rule and drops anything not allowed earlier. AllowInternetOutBound has priority 65001 and allows outbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet tag, which is why VMs have outbound internet access by default. Wrong: 100 is the lowest priority number available for CUSTOM rules, not a default rule. 65500 belongs to the DenyAll rules in both directions, not to the Allow defaults. 4096 is the highest priority number for a custom rule and is never used by a default rule. An Allow action for DenyAllOutBound would contradict the rule's purpose and its name.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A virtual machine resides in a subnet that has a network security group associated with it, and the virtual machine's network interface also has a network security group associated with it. You are documenting how Azure filters traffic for this virtual machine. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: For inbound traffic to the virtual machine, Azure first evaluates: [the NSG associated with the subnet | the NSG associated with the network interface | the NSG that contains the rule with the lowest priority number]
opzione_b: For outbound traffic from the virtual machine, Azure first evaluates: [the NSG associated with the subnet | the NSG associated with the network interface | both NSGs simultaneously]
opzione_c: Maximum number of network security groups that can be associated with a single subnet: [0 | 1 | 2]
opzione_d: When traffic matches a security rule, Azure: [stops processing further rules | continues evaluating all remaining rules | applies the most restrictive matching rule]
risposta_corretta: the NSG associated with the subnet,the NSG associated with the network interface,1,stops processing further rules
spiegazione: Correct: For inbound traffic Azure processes the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG; for outbound traffic the order is reversed, with the NIC NSG evaluated first and then the subnet NSG. Each subnet and each network interface can have zero or one NSG associated with it, so the maximum for a single subnet is 1 (the same NSG may be reused across many subnets and NICs). Once traffic matches a rule, processing stops, which means lower-priority rules with the same attributes are never processed. Wrong: Priority numbers are only compared within a single NSG; they never determine which NSG is evaluated first across the subnet/NIC boundary. The two NSGs are not evaluated simultaneously; the order is deterministic and direction-dependent. Continuing to evaluate all remaining rules, or picking the most restrictive match, describes other firewall products, not the first-match-wins model that Azure NSGs use.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: Subnet-1 in VNet1 is associated with a network security group named nsg-sub. The network interface of vm-1, which resides in Subnet-1, is associated with a network security group named nsg-nic. nsg-sub contains a single custom inbound rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source Internet, destination Any, destination port 443. nsg-nic contains a single custom inbound rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source 198.51.100.5, destination Any, destination port 22. Neither network security group contains any other custom rule. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: Inbound TCP 443 from a client on the internet to vm-1 is: [Allowed | Denied]
opzione_b: Inbound TCP 22 from the internet host 198.51.100.5 to vm-1 is: [Allowed | Denied]
opzione_c: Inbound TCP 443 from another virtual machine in VNet1 to vm-1 is: [Allowed | Denied]
opzione_d: To allow SSH from 198.51.100.5 to reach vm-1, you must add an allow rule to: [nsg-nic only | nsg-sub only | both nsg-sub and nsg-nic]
spiegazione: Correct: (a) Denied. nsg-sub is evaluated first and its rule at priority 100 allows TCP 443, but nsg-nic is then evaluated and contains no rule matching TCP 443 from the internet, so its DenyAllInBound default rule at 65500 drops the traffic. For inbound traffic to reach the VM, the port must be open in BOTH NSGs. (b) Denied. nsg-sub is evaluated first; no rule matches TCP 22, so DenyAllInBound in nsg-sub drops the traffic before nsg-nic is ever evaluated, even though nsg-nic would have allowed it. (c) Allowed. The custom rule in nsg-sub does not match (its source is the Internet tag, not the VirtualNetwork tag), so the AllowVNetInBound default rule at 65000 permits the flow in nsg-sub; the same default rule in nsg-nic permits it as well. (d) nsg-sub only. nsg-nic already allows TCP 22 from 198.51.100.5 at priority 100, so only the subnet NSG is missing the rule. Wrong: Adding the rule to nsg-nic only would leave the subnet NSG blocking the traffic, and adding it to both is unnecessary because nsg-nic already permits it.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: A network security group named nsg-web is associated with the subnet named Subnet-Web in VNet1. nsg-web contains one custom inbound rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source Internet, destination the application security group asg-web, destination port 80. No other custom rules exist. VM1 and VM2 both reside in Subnet-Web, and neither of their network interfaces has a network security group associated with it. The network interface of VM1 is a member of asg-web. The network interface of VM2 is not a member of any application security group. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true. 1) Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM1. 2) Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM2. 3) VM1 can connect to VM2 over TCP port 80 across the virtual network.
opzione_a: Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM1.
opzione_b: Inbound HTTP traffic from the internet reaches VM2.
opzione_c: VM1 can connect to VM2 over TCP port 80 across the virtual network.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: VM1's network interface is a member of asg-web, so the rule at priority 100 that specifies asg-web as the destination applies to it, and inbound TCP 80 from the internet is allowed. Statement 2 - No: Network interfaces that are members of an application security group apply the rules that specify that group as the source or destination; the rule does not affect other network interfaces. Because VM2's NIC is not a member of asg-web, the rule at priority 100 does not match, and the DenyAllInBound default rule at priority 65500 drops the traffic, even though nsg-web is associated with the whole subnet. Statement 3 - Yes: For this intra-virtual-network flow the rule at priority 100 does not match, because its source is the Internet service tag and its destination is asg-web. The next matching rule is the AllowVNetInBound default rule at priority 65000, which allows communication between resources in the virtual network, so VM1 can reach VM2 on TCP 80.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: VM3 resides in a subnet that is associated with a network security group named nsg-sub, and VM3's network interface is associated with a network security group named nsg-nic. nsg-nic contains an outbound custom rule: priority 150, Deny, TCP, source Any, destination Internet, destination port 443. nsg-sub contains an outbound custom rule: priority 100, Allow, TCP, source Any, destination Internet, destination port 443. VM3 attempts to establish an outbound HTTPS connection to a public endpoint. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true. 1) VM3 can currently establish the outbound HTTPS connection. 2) Changing the priority of the allow rule in nsg-sub from 100 to 50 will allow the connection. 3) Deleting the deny rule from nsg-nic will allow the connection.
opzione_a: VM3 can currently establish the outbound HTTPS connection.
opzione_b: Changing the priority of the allow rule in nsg-sub from 100 to 50 will allow the connection.
opzione_c: Deleting the deny rule from nsg-nic will allow the connection.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: For outbound traffic, Azure evaluates the NSG associated with the network interface first. nsg-nic denies TCP 443 to the Internet tag at priority 150, so the traffic is dropped and nsg-sub never receives it. Statement 2 - No: This is the classic misconception. Priority numbers are only compared between rules WITHIN the same network security group; they do not determine which NSG is evaluated first. Lowering the number to 50 in nsg-sub changes nothing, because nsg-nic is still evaluated first for outbound traffic and still denies the flow. Statement 3 - Yes: With the deny rule removed, nsg-nic no longer has a matching custom rule, so its AllowInternetOutBound default rule at priority 65001 allows the traffic. nsg-sub is then evaluated and its allow rule at priority 100 permits TCP 443 to the Internet tag, so the connection succeeds.

sotto_argomento: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
domanda: Case study: Contoso runs a line-of-business application in a virtual network named VNet1. A single subnet named Subnet-App hosts both the web servers and the application servers of the workload, and a network security group named nsg-app is associated with Subnet-App. The web servers must accept inbound TCP port 443 from the internet. The application servers, which are in the same subnet, must never accept inbound traffic from the internet. Contoso frequently scales the web tier in and out, so the private IP addresses of the web servers change often. The security team requires that no network security group be associated with individual network interfaces, and that the number of security rules be kept to a minimum. You need to allow inbound HTTPS to the web servers only. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create an application security group named asg-web, add the network interfaces of the web servers to it, and add a rule to nsg-app that allows TCP 443 with the source set to the Internet service tag and the destination set to asg-web
opzione_b: Associate a second network security group with the network interfaces of the application servers, and add a rule to it that denies TCP 443 from the Internet service tag
opzione_c: Add a rule to nsg-app that allows TCP 443 with the source set to the Internet service tag and the destination set to the VirtualNetwork service tag
opzione_d: Move the web servers to a dedicated subnet and create a route table that sends inbound internet traffic for the application servers to None
spiegazione: Correct: An application security group lets you group network interfaces by role and use the group as the destination of a security rule, so the policy follows the VMs as the web tier scales and IP addresses change. Only network interfaces that are members of asg-web apply the rule; the application server NICs are unaffected and remain protected by the DenyAllInBound default rule. This satisfies every requirement: no NIC-level NSG, minimal rules, and no IP maintenance. Wrong: Associating an NSG with the application server NICs violates the stated requirement that no NSG be associated with individual network interfaces, and it adds ongoing administrative overhead. Setting the destination to the VirtualNetwork service tag would allow TCP 443 from the internet to every resource in the virtual network address space, including the application servers, which breaks the security requirement. A route table controls where packets are forwarded, not whether they are permitted; user-defined routes cannot filter inbound internet traffic in place of a security rule, and moving the web servers is unnecessary work.

sotto_argomento: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
domanda: Case study: Fabrikam hosts a reporting application on a virtual machine named vm-1 in a resource group named rg-1. vm-1 is running and resides in a subnet that is associated with a network security group named nsg-subnet. The network interface of vm-1, named nic-1, is associated with a different network security group named nsg-nic. Both network security groups have been edited by several administrators over time and now contain dozens of custom rules. Users report that they cannot reach the application on TCP port 8080. An administrator needs to review, in a single output, the aggregation of all rules from both network security groups that currently apply to nic-1, by using the Azure CLI. Which command should the administrator run?
opzione_a: az network nsg rule list --resource-group rg-1 --nsg-name nsg-subnet
opzione_b: az network nic list-effective-nsg --resource-group rg-1 --name nic-1
opzione_c: az network watcher show-next-hop --resource-group rg-1 --vm vm-1 --source-ip 10.0.0.4 --dest-ip 10.0.1.4 --nic nic-1
opzione_d: az network nsg show --resource-group rg-1 --name nsg-nic
spiegazione: Correct: az network nic list-effective-nsg returns the effective security rules for a network interface, which are the aggregation of the rules in the NSG associated with the network interface and the NSG associated with the subnet the network interface is in. This is exactly the single consolidated view the administrator needs, and it works because vm-1 is running (output is only returned when the VM is in the running state and at least one NSG is associated). Wrong: az network nsg rule list returns only the custom rules of the one NSG you name, so it shows neither the default rules nor the rules of the other NSG. az network watcher show-next-hop returns routing information (the next hop type and IP address); it does not evaluate security rules. az network nsg show returns the details of a single NSG, so it again omits the second NSG and does not produce an aggregated effective rule set.
